listings.name: Plaza de la Bellas Artes
listings.content: Commonly known as Palace of Fine Arts or Cathedral of Arts in Mexico, host of art events and art exhibitions, along with a number of enormous murals including Diego Rivera's El hombre controlador del universo and Jorge González Camarena's Liberación.

listings.name: Plaza de la Constitución
listings.content: Commonly known as Zócalo, it is one of the largest squares in the world, surrounded by historic buildings, including the City Hall and the Cathedral.

listings.name: Catedral Metropolitana de la Ciudad de México
listings.content: Next to El Zocalo in the city center. The biggest cathedral in the Americas. Containing many altars, its principal altar is made from solid gold.

listings.name: Angel de la Independencia
listings.content: A monument in Reforma Avenue that celebrates Mexico's independence in 1810.

listings.name: Basílica de Guadalupe
listings.content: Catholicism's holiest place in the Americas, and the destination of pilgrims from all over the world, especially during the yearly celebration on the 12th of December. It is the shrine that guards the poncho of Juan Diego that contains the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, and is in the northernmost part of the city.

listings.name: Ciudad Universitaria
listings.content: The main campus of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Located on Insurgentes Sur Avenue, it is one of the world's largest universities, with more than 270,000 students every semester. In 2007 it was declared a .

listings.name: Coyoacán
listings.content: Historic Colonial Arts district which was home to Frida Kahlo, Leon Trotsky, and Diego Rivera, among others.

listings.name: Plaza Garibaldi-Mariachi
listings.content: The square is surrounded by cafés and restaurants much favored by tourists, and in these and in the square itself groups of musicians play folk music. Most of these groups are "mariachis" from Jalisco, dressed in Charro costume and playing trumpets, violins, guitars and the guitarrón or bass guitar.

listings.name: Paseo de la Reforma
listings.content: A 12 km long grand avenue built for the Emperor Maximilian's wife in the 19th century. Its name commemorates the liberal reforms of Mexican President Benito Juarez.

listings.name: Cineteca Nacional
listings.content: It was the first to screen art films, and is known for its forums, retrospectives and homages. It has four screening rooms, a video and a film library, as well as a cafeteria.

listings.name: Torre Latinoamericana
listings.content: For stunning views of the city. Its central location, height (183 m or 597 ft; 45 stories), and history make it one of Mexico City's most important landmarks.

listings.name: National Museum of Anthropology
listings.content: One of the best museums worldwide over, it was built in late 1960s and designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez. Notice the huge, impressive fountain in the courtyard. It gathers the best collection of sculptures, jewels and handcrafts from ancient Mexican cultures, and could take many hours to see everything. They also have interesting international special exhibits.

listings.name: Plaza de las Tres Culturas
listings.content: Examples of modern, colonial, and pre-Columbian architecture, all around one square.

listings.name: Museum of Modern Art
listings.content: Here you will find paintings from Frida Kahlo, Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo, as well as a sculpture garden.

listings.name: Dolores Olmedo Museum
listings.content: An art philanthropist left her former home, the grand Hacienda La Noria, as a museum featuring the works of her friend Diego Rivera. At least 137 of his works are displayed here, as are 25 paintings of Frida Kahlo. The premises also feature beautiful gardens full of peacocks and a weird species of Aztec dog. However, the museum is under renovation and is sched to reopen sometime in 2026.

listings.name: Fine Arts Palace Museum
listings.content: A concert hall and an arts center, it houses some of Mexico's finest murals and the Art Deco interior is worth seeing alone.

listings.name: Museo Soumaya
listings.content: A private museum and collection of many well-known European artists, including an extensive selection of works by Auguste Rodin.

listings.name: Rufino Tamayo Museum
listings.content: Contains the works of Mexican painter, Rufino Tamayo.

listings.name: José Luis Cuevas Museum
listings.content: Opened in 1992 and is filled with about 1,000 paintings, drawings, and sculptures from notorious artist, Jose Cuevas.

listings.name: National History Museum in Chapultepec's Castle
listings.content: The Museum's nineteen rooms contain, in addition to a collection of pre-Columbian material and reproductions of old manuscripts, a vast range of exhibits illustrating the history of Mexico since the Spanish conquest.

listings.name: Papalote Children's Museum
listings.content: If you've got kids, they'll love it! Bright, colorful, and filled with educational experiences for children of all ages.

listings.name: Universum
listings.content: A science museum maintained by UNAM, the largest university in Latin America. Take some time to wander around the Campus.

listings.name: Casa Mural Diego Rivera
listings.content: Contains murals of acclaimed artist, Diego Rivera.

listings.name: National Palace (Zocalo)
listings.content: You can see some impressive Diego Rivera frescoes.

listings.name: San Idelfonso Museum
listings.content: There are some of Orozco's best frescoes. The temporary exhibitions are usually very good.

listings.name: Franz Meyer Museum
listings.content: Display the collections of Franz Mayer, it holds Mexico's largest decorative art collection and also hosts temporary exhibits in the fields of design and photography.

listings.name: Mexico City's Museum
listings.content: Great place to learn about Mexico City's eclectic history.

listings.name: Templo Mayor Museum (Zocalo)
listings.content: Contains the ruins and last remnants of the Aztec empire. attached to the huge archeological site where the foundations of the temple were accidentally found in the 1970s.

listings.name: San Carlos Museum
listings.content: The San Carlos Museum holds some of Mexico's best paintings and exhibit 15th and 16th century paintings.

listings.name: National Art Museum
listings.content: The National Art Museum, houses a rich collection of Mexican art ranging from the 16th to the first half of the 20th centuries.

listings.name: Frida Kahlo Museum
listings.content: The former house of the painter since she was born to her death, and full of some of her works, and many of her personal artifacts.

listings.name: Anahuacalli Museum
listings.content: An impressive modern representation of Mayan architecture, it houses Diego Rivera’s collection of Aztec and other precolumbian cultures' sculptures.

listings.name: Leon Trotsky Museum
listings.content: This was the house where Trotsky lived in exile during the last 1.5 years of his life, and was murdered by one of Stalin's agents. Guided tours are provided by members of the Workers/ Revolutionary Party.

listings.name: Wise Men's day
listings.content: Most Mexican kids receive toys from the Three Wise Men (Reyes Magos). This is a celebration that pays homage to the aforementioned Bible story. To celebrate it the family gather to eat the "Rosca de Reyes", a sort of bundt cake filled with plastic baby Jesus figures. Traditionally, people who get a figure in their slice of cake are expected to host a feast with tamales on Candelaria Day, February 2. The surroundings of the Alameda Central park are filled with costumed Reyes Magos on the days leading to January 6.

listings.name: Art Week
listings.content: Each year in February, the world of contemporary art focuses on Mexico City's Art Week when parties, celebrations, special gallery exhibitions and myriad galas take place throughout the city. The event takes place at the same time as two other major art events, ZsONA MACO, and Feria Material as well as numerous other events at galleries and museums throughout the city.

listings.name: Independence Day "Yell"
listings.content: In the evening, the President of the country (or the city mayor) salutes the crowds from the presidential balcony in the National Palace in the Constitution Square (Zocalo) and shouts the famous "Viva Mexico". The Zocalo (and the rest of the city) is decorated with ornaments and lights. This is an incredible expression of Mexican patriotism combined with a party mood. Expect big crowds with a big revelery. If you want smaller crowds, the squares at the center of every borough usually host similar celebrations.

listings.name: Independence Parade
listings.content: In the morning, there is a military parade that runs across Paseo de la Reforma, turns right at Juarez Avenue which later becomes Madero Street and ends at the Zocalo. 15,000 to 30,000 soldiers of the Mexican Army, Navy and Air Force march through the streets displaying its equipment and weapons.

listings.name: Alebrijes Parade
listings.content: Alebrijes are brightly colored fanciful animal figures that are one of Mexico's most iconic pop art genres. Each year, enormous Alebrijes floats are created and a parade is held along Paseo de la Reforma and then on to the Zocalo. Pink polka-dotted pigs, Purple-winged dragons, orange dogs with spiked haircuts....these and more will march in the parade. After the parade, the giant Alebrijes will be placed in plazas and public spaces along Avenida Reforma for a 3-4 week period when the public can get up close to take their Instagram-ready selfies.

listings.name: Day of the Dead
listings.content: Mexico is one of the few countries in the world that celebrates this day (Dia de los Muertos), in which people go to the cemeteries to offer tribute to their departed ones, and decorate their graves with marigolds and bright colors. But this is not a sad celebration, on the contrary, people give family and friends candy treats in the shape of skulls and bones made of sugar and chocolate, as well as delicious bread called "Pan de Muerto". Don't miss a visit to a public market to find these delicacies, and watch out for the parades to and from the local cemeteries. In Mexico City, festivities include the lively Desfile de Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead Parade) which was inspired by the James Bond movie, Spectre. The parade includes people dressed as calaveras catrinas and huge colorful alebrije balloon as well as floats and marching bands. The parade route goes up Reforma and over to the Zocalo. In Xochimilco, there are Day of the Dead parties on the canals and the already colorful trajineras are decked out in marigolds, skeletons and wildly fanciful themes.

listings.name: Six Flags Mexico
listings.content: Largest amusement park in Latin America. The park is fitted with several million-dollar attractions, including Batman the Ride and not for the faint-hearted Medusa Roller Coaster.

listings.name: Parque Aztlan
listings.content: Small urban amusement park in the heart of Chapultepec Park. Park entry is free but rides are paid for individually. Includes a giant Ferris wheel with 40 cabins, a large steel roller coaster, a carousel, and swings.

listings.name: Estadio Azteca
listings.content: The largest stadium in Latin America is also the eighth biggest soccer stadium in the world. It's the home of El Tri, the Mexico men's national team, and also home to two of the country's most famous soccer top-tier professional clubs: Club América and Cruz Azul. It also serves as venue for concerts and for occasional NFL regular-season games outside the United States. The stadium is undergoing renovations as it prepares to host the opening games of the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

listings.name: Estadio Olimpico de Ciudad Universitaria
listings.content: Simply known as "Estadio de C.U." Located south of the city, this was the site of the 1968 Olympic opening ceremony. It is home to Club Universidad Nacional, more often known as Pumas, a soccer team operated by the National University (UNAM). The Pumas began as an amateur team of UNAM students, but are now a top-tier professional team in the Liga MX (though still owned and operated by the university). The stadium hosts several sports, mainly soccer and American football.

listings.name: Estadio Alfredo Harp Helu
listings.content: Modernistic baseball stadium built in 2019 for 20,000 cheering fans. It is home field for the Diablos de Mexico, a Mexican League professional team.

listings.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
listings.content: Built in 1962, this 4.4 km track hosts Grand Prix Formula One and other motor racing such as NASCAR and A1-Grand Prix. The next Formula 1 races are 29 October to 1 November 2026.

listings.name: Arena Ciudad de Mexico
listings.content: With a full capacity of 22,300, Arena CDMX hosts indoor sporting events and a wide range of popular music events. It is the home for annual NBA basketball games played in Mexico, and also hosts home games of Capitanes de la Ciudad de México, the country's representative in the NBA G League.

listings.name: Hipodromo de las Americas
listings.content: Mexico City's home for horse racing, both thoroughbreds and quarter-horses. There are races nearly every day, with different zones for different budgets.

listings.name: Arena México
listings.content: The most famous venue for lucha libre.

listings.name: Arena Coliseo
listings.content: Another famous venue for lucha libre and boxing.

listings.name: Bellas Artes
listings.content: Opera, traditional Mexican and classical music.

listings.name: Circo Volador
listings.content: Alternative music and metal.

listings.name: Ollin Yoliztli
listings.content: Home to the Mexico City Symphonic Orchestra.

listings.name: Sala Nezahualcóyotl
listings.content: Home to the UNAM Symphonic Orchestra

listings.name: Plaza de la Constitución
listings.content: This square measures 240m long on either side. A huge Mexican flag occupies the center, which is ceremoniously lowered and re-raised each day at 18:00. You may see art exhibits, concerts, demonstrations or all manner of social gatherings taking place here. On New Year's Day, practitioners of Mexico's indigenous religions gather to bless believers for the coming year; Mexican independence is celebrated in the plaza on 15 and 16 September. During December, through the miracle of modern refrigeration, the entire Zócalo is transformed into an ice skating rink.
listings.image: Plaza de la Constitución desde el Edificio de Gobierno.jpg

listings.name: Templo Mayor
listings.content: The site of the main Aztec temple of Tenochtitlan, it was destroyed by Spanish conquistadors in 1521, who then promptly erected the Cathedral roughly over it – but not quite. Centuries later, nearly completely forgotten, its actual location was discovered by accident in 1978 when electrical workers found a piece of a large stone disc depicting the goddess Coyolxauhqui. This set off a few furious years of archaeological digging, resulting in a rather surprising (and extremely significant) discovery that nested underneath the original Aztec temple was six distinct smaller, older temples. You can see each layer walking through the dig site.
listings.price: M$59, free for children under 12 and students with valid ID

listings.name: Museo del Templo Mayor
listings.content: This excellent four-story museum was designed by Mexican architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, and built in 1987 to showcase the many artifacts found on the site. Highlights include the Coyolxauhqui disc as well as the many thousands of offerings found during the still-ongoing excavation.

listings.name: Palacio Nacional
listings.content: The palace in its current form began construction in 1693 and served as the Palace of the Viceroy of New Spain until the Mexican War of Independence, when it became the executive seat of the President (though today it is no longer his official residence). The walls inside the palace display murals by Diego Rivera depicting the history of Mexico from the pre-Columbian age to the Mexican Revolution. You can also visit the Recinto Legislativo, a replica of the first Mexican Congress, and tour the home of Benito Juárez. Tours in English are free; ask for one at the information desk across the street. It’s strongly recommended to get there early in the day, and you’ll likely be given a reserved time to return later that afternoon.
listings.price: Free admission with photo ID (national driver's license is acceptable)

listings.name: Plaza de la Fundación
listings.content: This place is allegedly where the Aztecs found the eagle eating a snake on top of a cactus (nopal), the divine sign of the gods to settle down and establish the city of Tenochtitlán. It features a sculpture by Juan Olaguibel made in 1970.

listings.name: Nacional Monte de Piedad
listings.content: This building, which was completed in 1758, was built on the grounds of the house of Aztec emperor Moctezuma and later the residence of the Spanish conqueror Hernán Cortés. The building was acquired in 1838 by the Nacional Monte de Piedad, a pawn shop established in 1775 that still operates today.
listings.address: Monte de Piedad and Cinco de Mayo

listings.name: Casa de la Primera Imprenta de América
listings.content: This building, which dates from 1524, housed the first printing press in the New World, which operated from 1539 until 1560. After this time the building was used for a number of purposes until it was restored by the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana (UAM) in 1989; it now houses a museum displaying some of the first books printed in Mexico.

listings.name: Plaza Manuel Gamio
listings.content: Features an open-air diorama of the old Tenochtitlán.

listings.name: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación
listings.content: This building was completed in 1945 and was designed by architect Antonio Muñoz Garcia.
listings.image: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación de México - frontispicio.jpg

listings.name: Catedral Metropolitana de México
listings.content: The largest cathedral in the American continent. Designed by Claudio de Arcinieaga, construction started in 1537 and lasted for 250 years. Be sure to check out the side chapels where parishioners leave offerings for the various saints. For a bird's-eye view of the plaza, you can take a 40-minute tour (Spanish language only) of the upper levels and bell towers of the cathedral (M$12).

listings.name: Sagrario Metropolitano
listings.content: A side chapel next to the Cathedral completed in 1769. The façade is an excellent example of Mexican Churrigueresque architecture.

listings.name: Templo de San Francisco
listings.content: This church was started in the 16th century and completed in the 19th century; it was built in the grounds of the zoo of Aztec Emperor Moctezuma.
listings.image: Segunda sección capilla de San Francisco 1.JPG

listings.name: Templo Expiatorio Nacional de San Felipe de Jesús
listings.content: Built in 1897 on the site of the former Vasque Church of Aranzazu.
listings.image: Fachada del Templo de San Felipe de JesúsD.jpg

listings.name: Santa Teresa La Antigua
listings.content: Built in 1678 and refurbished in 1845.
listings.image: Fachada y campanario del Ex Convento de Santa Teresa.JPG

listings.name: Templo de la Enseñanza
listings.content: Tucked away on a side street, this very narrow gem of a church was built in the 1770s and is notable for being an outstanding example of Mexican Churrigueresque architecture. Even more remarkable than the façade, however, are the nine gilt retablos inside.

listings.name: Templo y Convento de Regina Coeli
listings.content: Huge historic church known for its opulent baroque interior. Part of a large Conceptionist convent founded in 1573. The statues and artwork is spectacular as is the gilded altar.

listings.name: Templo de San Felipe Neri
listings.content: Baroque-style church established by the Jesuit order in the late 16th century and completed in 1610. The church is famous for its extensive art collection, some of which is on display for public viewing in an attached art gallery. The art was commissioned by the Jesuits during their first two centuries in Mexico. The collection remained intact when the Jesuits were expelled from all lands of the Spanish Empire during the 18th century. The building itself is admired for its early baroque architecture, which was more restrained than the effusive opulence of later churches, but that restraint did not extend to the church interior, which features many sculptures and period oil paintings, as well as architectural details like the extravangant Neoclassical main altar (designed by Manuel Tolsa to replace the original altar), covered in gold leaf. The art collection is one of the largest collections of early Mexican art and the gallery features four salons. Salon 1 contains the earliest works in the collection, mostly by well-known artists in Spain. Salon 2 boldly features a huge painting of Saint Philip Neri and the room is dedicated to works associated with the saint, as well as portraits of 11 popes. Salon 3 is a historical perspective of religious art from the 17th through 19th century with paintings depicting Biblical scenes and portraits of saints from those centuries. Salon 4 features works from the 18th century with two prominent paintings by Miguel Correa, one showing the torments of hell and the second showing judgment day as the good are separated from the evil.

listings.name: Alameda Central
listings.content: Established in 1592, this green garden with fountains and statues is the oldest public park in the Americas. The name comes from álamo, the Spanish word for poplar tree, that were planted here. Much of the current layout of the park, with its starburst pattern of paths around fountains and the central kiosk dates from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

listings.name: Plaza de Santo Domingo
listings.content: The second largest square in Centro Histórico after the Zócalo. It is surrounded by various important buildings such as the Palacio de la Inquisición, Santo Domingo convent and the old Customs House.
listings.image: Fuente de la Plaza de Santo Domingo.JPG

listings.name: Museo de la Medicina Mexicana
listings.content: This museum managed by the Medicine Faculty of the National University shows the history of health care in Mexico. Features a great replica of an old pharmacy and reconstructed labs of influential medical researchers. Signage is in Spanish only. It is housed in the Inquisition Palace, built between 1732 and 1737, which was the head office of the Holy Inquisition, the religious authority famous for torturing heretic people.

listings.name: Plaza Manuel Tolsá
listings.content: In this beautiful square you can find the statue of Spanish king Charles IV also known as El Caballito (the little horse).
listings.image: Estatua del Caballito en la Plaza Manuel Tolsá Noche y Luna.JPG

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Arte
listings.content: Housed in the former Palace of Telecommunications, this beautiful Porfirian-style building was built in 1904 by architect Silvio Contri. The museum presents a permanent collection of paintings and sculptures from the 16th century through the early 20th century, including a large number of very early Mexican paintings. The museum is famous for its enormous and ostentatiously decorated Reception Hall and for its Patio de los Leones, which houses much of its sculpture collection. The museum is very large with over 3,000 objects on display. It often hosts temporary exhibits on special subjects. Allow at least a half day to fully explore its many galleries.
listings.price: Adult M$95; children under 13, people with disabilities, students with a valid ID: free; photography permit (no flash or tripod) M$5, video permit (no tripod or lighting) M$30

listings.name: Palacio de Minería
listings.content: Formerly the Mining College, this building dated from 1792 features an old library and a chapel. It serves as venue for the yearly Mexico City Book Fair.

listings.name: Plaza de las Tres Culturas
listings.content: So called because in one city square you can see three different time periods of Mexico City's development mixed together: the pre-hispanic Aztec temple grounds of Tlatelolco, the 16th-century Spanish Church of Santiago, and a modern 20th-century skyscraper, now home of the University Cultural Center Tlatelolco (CCUT) for UNAM.

listings.name: Zona Arquelógica Tlatelolco
listings.content: The temple, like Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, was built in several layers and is now the site of continuing archaeological exploration; it occupies the largest amount of area, on the north and west side of the plaza. If you're not around for the tour, you can guide yourself along the path (complete with English plaques) that takes you through the ruins, which deposits you in front of the Church of Santiago, on the east side of the plaza.

listings.name: Templo de Santiago
listings.content: The colonial church, built by Spaniards immediately after destroying the temple in their conquest of Aztec lands, was constructed using stones "borrowed" from the temple itself. Despite its weathered appearance, the interior is well-maintained and should still hold regular Mass, although doors may not always be open to the public.
listings.image: Iglesia de Santiago Tlatelolco, México D.F., México, 2013-10-16, DD 38.JPG

listings.name: Centro Cultural Universitario Tlatelolco
listings.content: To the south, you'll see the modern-day tower and its adjacent buildings, which were built for the Secretary of External Relations (SRE), now headquartered across the street (though they still have offices in the church's adjoining cloister). UNAM runs the building as a conference hall and cultural center, and has a few exhibits open to the public: Memorial 68 (see Museums, below) and the Blaisten Collection, showcasing modern art.

listings.name: Plaza Garibaldi
listings.content: In this square, groups of musicians play folk music. Most of these groups are "mariachis" from Jalisco, dressed in Charro costume and playing trumpets, violins, guitars and the guitarrón or bass guitar. The square is surrounded by cafés and restaurants that cater to mariachi band enthusiasts.

listings.name: Museo de Arte Popular
listings.content: The Museo de Arte Popular in Mexico City is a vibrant showcase of folk art from every Mexican state, housed in a stunning 1920s art deco former fire station designed by Vicente Mendiola. Spread across three levels and five thematic halls, it displays crafts like Chiapas carnaval masks, Oaxaca alebrijes, regional costumes, and Day of the Dead artifacts. An illustrated wall map highlights Mexico’s regional traditions. Even museum skeptics and kids love its colorful exhibits, and the ground-level shop offers unique, high-quality handicrafts.

listings.name: Museo Franz Mayer
listings.content: Housed in an 18th-century building, houses the largest and finest collection of decorative arts in Mexico. The collection, including objects from Mexico, Europe and Asia ranging from the 16th to the 19th century was a donation of German-Mexican philanthropist Franz Mayer.

listings.name: Museo José Luis Cuevas
listings.content: Housed in the former convent of Santa Ines built in 1600. The museum's collection features works by Mexican artist Jose Luis Cuevas as well as other modern artists, it also presents works (especially sculptures) from European artists such as Picasso and Rembrandt. The museum's courtyard features an enormous statue called, appropriately enough, La Gigantesca.

listings.name: Academía de San Carlos
listings.content: Housed in a building dated 1785 that was conceived as the Royal Academy of Beaux Arts. It is administered by the National University and features permanent and temporary painting collections. This is the oldest arts academy in the Americas and has trained large number of Mexico's most famous artists. Today, the academy is part of the Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (UNAM) and only graduate courses are taught in the historic centro.

listings.name: Museo Mural Diego Rivera
listings.content: This museum was built to house Diego Rivera's famous mural Sueño de una tarde dominical en la Alameda Central ('Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central'), which the painter created for the Hotel del Prado in 1947-1948. The hotel was destroyed in the earthquake of 1985, but the mural survived and was moved to this location. The museum also hosts permanent and temporary exhibits.

listings.name: Museo Nacional de la Estampa
listings.content: Features a collection of old engravings and other graphic arts.
listings.price: M$45 (adults), free (students/teachers/INAPAM members); free admission on Sundays
listings.image: De noche fuera del Museo Nacional de la Estampa.JPG

listings.name: Museo Kaluz
listings.content: Eclectic art museum that straddles the line between traditional artistic styles and the worlds of modern and contemporary art. The museum focuses on works that reflect the history and changing cultural values of Mexico City, a unique collection in a city crowded with outstanding arts venues. The museum itself is housed in a historic building, originally the Hospedería de Santo Tomás de Villanueva, but known to generations of Mexicans as the Hotel Cortes, the building was extensively restored and updated prior to the opening of Museo Kaluz in 2021. Roof top terrace with peaceful gardens and a popular cafe.

listings.name: Museo de la Arte de SHCP
listings.content: Eclectic art collection owned by the government's Finance ministry. Mexico has an innovative tax program that allows collectors and artists to pay tax debts by donating significant artworks. The collection includes works by famous artists like Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo, and Rufino Tamayo as well as many cutting-edge contemporary works.

listings.name: Museo Vivo del Muralismo
listings.content: This museum is housed in a former convent from 1729 that later became headquarters for the Education Secretariat. In 1923, the department commissioned the up-and-coming Diego Rivera to decorate the building with 124 mural panels, extending over two city blocks and filling three levels. There are elaborate panels of traditional Mexican life on the ground floor, state seals on the second floor, and themes of revolution and class inequality on the third level. There is also a David Alfaro Siqueiros mural in the main stairwell. In 2024, the building became a museum dedicated to Mexican murals, with additional exhibits. Photography permitted, no flash.
listings.image: Diego Rivera Murals - Secretaria de Educacion Publica (SEP).jpg

listings.name: Museo de la Ciudad de México
listings.content: This museum presents the history of the city in an 18th-century mansion; the building is possibly more interesting than the contents. It is believed that a conquistador's house used to be on the site, as evidenced by the southwest cornerstone of an Aztec serpent head likely taken from the Templo Mayor.
listings.price: M$29 (adults), M$14.50 (students/teachers/INAPAM members); free on W
listings.image: Museo de la Ciudad de México, México D.F., México, 2013-10-16, DD 130.JPG

listings.name: Memorial del 68
listings.content: In UNAM's University Cultural Center Tlatelolco (CCUT) at the Plaza de las Tres Culturas (see Landmarks, above), Memorial 68 is a well-put together museum chronicling the events surrounding the police massacre of student protesters at Tlatelolco in 1968, around the time of the Summer Olympics, which were hosted in Mexico City that year. It's definitely worth a look, but all explanatory text and video interviews are in Spanish only, so brush up your vocabulary or bring a translator.
listings.price: M$30 (adults), M$15 (students), free (children under 6); free admission on Su

listings.name: Museo Memoria y Tolerancia
listings.content: Opened in 2010, this museum is dedicated to the remembrance of genocides and crimes against humanity committed around the globe, with the goal of promoting peace and tolerance. Separate sections of the museum are devoted to the Holocaust, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rwanda, the Khmer Rouge, Darfur, Armenia, and Guatemala. Genocide is only one of the issues the museum confronts. Exhibits also explore hate crimes committed in the name of religion, racial purity, and especially sexual orientation, with a number of exhibits and lectures exploring LGBT issues (in Mexico, they tend to add a lot of extra letters so that you might see it as LGBTTTQIA).
listings.price: M$75 (adults), M$60 (students/teachers/seniors); temporary exhibits: M$30 (adults), M$15 (concessions)

listings.name: Museo de la Indumentaria Mexicana
listings.content: Collection of traditional Mexican clothing.

listings.name: Museo del Calzado El Borceguí
listings.content: Private collection of old shoes from the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries. The museum belongs to the shoe store El Borcegui, established in 1865 and still selling shoes today.

listings.name: Museo Nacional de las Culturas
listings.content: Housed in the former Mint building built in 1734. The museum is dedicated to anthropology of the world.

listings.name: Museo Archivo de la Fotografia
listings.content: Housed in the historic 16th-century Casa de las Ajaracas, it is a rare survivor on a street that has seen other historic structures knocked down to explore the Templo Mayor site. The museum is home to a huge collection of historical photographs from the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries, documenting the constantly changing cityscape of Mexico City.

listings.name: Centro Cultural de España en México
listings.content: This is the official cultural center from the Spanish Embassy and features temporary exhibits.

listings.name: Museo de San Ildefonso
listings.content: Managed by the National University, this museum features some stunning murals and hosts great permanent and temporary art exhibits.
listings.price: M$50 (adults), M$25 (students/teachers), free (children under 12); free admission on Tu

listings.name: Museo del Estanquillo
listings.content: One of the newest museums in the city, this contains the personal collection of paintings, photography, and books of the Mexican journalist and writer Carlos Monsivais.

listings.name: Museo de la Caricatura
listings.content: Depicting the history of Mexican cartoons (political and amusing cartoons).

listings.name: Museo de la Luz
listings.content: Managed by the National University, this museum is mostly for students on everything to do with light (photography, electricity, vision, etc).

listings.name: Museo de la Charrería
listings.content: This museum features everything about the Mexican Cowboy, known as Charro.

listings.name: Museo Legislativo
listings.content: Museum dedicated to Mexico's Congress, with exhibits about the legislative process and the two houses: the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. The building houses the legislative chamber of the larger house (Chamber of Deputies). The Senate conducts sessions in a different building on Av. Reforma. Congressional tours are conducted through the museum and include the opportunity to enter the Chamber of Deputies. This building is equivalent to Parliament in London or the Capitol in Washington D.C.
listings.address: Honorable Congreso de la Unión #66, Col. Delegacion

listings.name: Centro de la Imagen
listings.content: This is one of Mexico City's premier exhibition spaces for photography, with rotating exhibits of work by Mexican and international photographers. The center also has a small bookstore.

listings.name: Palacio de Iturbide
listings.content: One of the oldest buildings in town, built in the late 16th century, it was first home to the local nobility and later the residence of Mexican Emperor Agustin de Iturbide. The building is owned today by the Cultural Trust of Banco Nacional de Mexico, the Mexican branch of Citibank.

listings.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
listings.content: Designed by Italian architect Adamo Boari. Construction started in 1905, however due to the Revolution War, it was not completed until 1934. The building is so heavy that it has sunk 4½m into the former lakebed. It is considered to be one of the best examples of Mexican Art Deco architecture; architectural and interior features include its copper cupolas and a Tiffany stained-glass stage curtain designed by Mexican painter Gerardo Murillo (commonly known as Dr. Atl).
listings.price: Free (lobby), M$60 for mezzanine with murals and galleries; $M30 photography permit; free admission on Sundays

listings.name: Palacio Postal
listings.content: One of the most beautiful buildings in the country and considered a National Heritage Building. Built in 1906, this European style building houses the main post office. Most of the materials used to build it were brought from Italy.
listings.image: Palacio Postal, México D.F., México, 2013-10-16, DD 52.JPG

listings.name: Museo Postal
listings.content: Housed in the Postal Palace, features old postal stationery and mail boxes.

listings.name: Banco de México
listings.content: Office of the Mexican Central Bank, built in 1925.
listings.address: Cinco de Mayo and Avda Eje Central

listings.name: Casa Rivas Mercado
listings.content: Architecturally unique and utterly fascinating restored neoclassical mansion from the Porfiriato era of the 19th century with period furnishings. Guided tours (in Spanish).

listings.name: Torre Latinoamericana
listings.content: Construction started in 1948 and was completed in 1956. This was Mexico's first skyscraper, boasting 44 floors and 182 meters. There is an observatory in the 42nd floor.

listings.name: Biblioteca Miguel Lerdo de Tejada
listings.content: This Baroque building was built as a church, but in the 1960s was repurposed to house a library. For visitors the primary interest is a series of enormous murals painted by the Russian emigré painter Vladimir Kibalchich Russakov (known in Mexico simply as Vlady). The murals in the main room are titled La Revolución y los Elementos (or 'Revolution and the Elements'). They required eight years to complete and are considered to be among the artist's most well-known works.

listings.name: Biblioteca de México José Vasconcelos
listings.content: Located in a former tobacco factory, it is one of the largest libraries in the city. It contains several beautiful courtyards and smaller libraries decorated according to the character of different Mexican authors who donated their book collections to the library.

listings.name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
listings.content: Next to Buenavista train station, it is the largest library in Mexico and functions as a central library for other libraries in the country. It is housed in an impressive modern building designed by architects Alberto Kalach and Juan Palomar. It is a must for visitors with an interest in architecture, not only for its stunning exterior design, but for its famous "floating stacks" that create the illusion of book shelves hanging from the ceiling. The library also houses a large contemporary art collection. The ground floor houses free temporary exhibits and the grounds include a botanical garden with native plants.
listings.image: Biblioteca Vasconcelos, Ciudad de México, México, 2015-07-20, DD 04-06 HDR.JPG

listings.name: Colonia Santa María la Ribera
listings.content: A colonia in the Cuauhtémoc borough, 2 km west of the historic center. This area was designated as a "Barrio Mágico" by the city in 2011. It was created in the late 19th century and reached its height between 1910 and 1930. In the 1930s, the middle class moved in and a new era of construction began. Today, the colonia is a mix of old mansions and homes (with over 1,000 categorized has having architectural or historic value), small shops and businesses, tenements and abandoned buildings.

listings.name: Alameda de Santa María la Ribera
listings.content: This historic park, established in 1861, is the heart of Santa María la Ribera. Its centerpiece is the Kiosco Morisco, an Art Nouveau pavilion built in 1884 for the New Orleans World’s Fair and relocated here in 1910. Surrounded by jacaranda trees and tiled fountains, it hosts dance classes, markets, and music on weekends.

listings.name: Museo del Instituto de Geología de la UNAM
listings.content: Housed in a 1906 Porfirian building in Santa María la Ribera, this museum showcases Mexico’s geological heritage with a mammoth skeleton, the dinosaur Isauria, and extensive mineral and fossil collections. Interactive exhibits and José María Velasco’s paintings enhance the experience.

listings.name: Parroquia Josefina de la Sagrada Familia
listings.content: This late 19th-century Byzantine-style church in Santa María la Ribera, designed by Carlos Herrera, is a hidden gem. Its vibrant interior features murals by Pedro Cruz depicting the life of St. Joseph, Christ’s birth, and the flight to Egypt, alongside stunning stained-glass windows and unique woodwork. A serene space for reflection, it’s a cultural treasure in one of Mexico City’s historic neighborhoods.

listings.name: Museo Universitario del Chopo
listings.content: Housed in a striking 1902 iron-and-glass building by Enrique Norten, this UNAM-managed museum in Santa María la Ribera focuses on contemporary art. It features rotating exhibits of avant-garde works, performances, and workshops. A cultural hub with a modernist vibe.

listings.name: Colonia Tabaclera
listings.content: A colonia in the Cuauhtémoc borough of Mexico City, on the western edge of the Centro Histórico and the Zona Rosa. This area was developed in the early 1900s with a mix of mansions and upscale apartment buildings, but its fortunes had declined by the end of the 20th century and the area is a bit rough at night with seedy characters engaged in prostitution, drug dealing, and petty crime, though it is generally safe during the day. The neighborhood has a bohemian character with several old cantinas. The neighborhood was once the refuge of Fidel Castro and his supporters who plotted their Cuban Revolution in local cantinas. The most famous attractions here are the Monument of the Revolution (with a large historical museum), the San Carlos National Museum, and the Jai-Alai Fronton Mexico.

listings.name: Teatro de la Ciudad
listings.content: Historic theatre that was built to resemble La Scala in Milan. It is a huge theatre with stacks of balcony levels looking onto the stage below. The best seats are on the 1st balcony level (better than main level seats). The theatre hosts a range of performances, many plays, but also dance, music, and other forms.

listings.name: Balet Folklorico
listings.content: Iconic performances of regional traditional dance and music from all parts of Mexico. The performance hall itself is a spectacular example of Art Deco architecture and features a stained glass curtain designed by famed muralist Dr. Atl.

listings.name: Arena Coliseo
listings.content: A famous venue for lucha libre (Mexican wrestling) and boxing.

listings.name: Avenida de República de Salvador
listings.content: The first half of the street (from Avenida Eje Central Avenue to Avenida Isabel la Católica) specializes in all sorts of electronics. From spare parts (speakers, wiring, transistors) to complete home theater systems, audio mixers and lighting for dance clubs. The other half of the street (from Isabel la Católica) specializes in stationery and paper.

listings.name: Calle del Artículo 123
listings.content: Specializes in appliances, from spare parts to industrial vacuums and blenders.

listings.name: Street food alley
listings.content: There is a big variety of street food.

listings.name: Food stall market
listings.content: At different times there are other food stalls open.

listings.name: Cocuyo's
listings.content: One of Mexico City's many famous taco stands, Cocuyo's has been featured on international food shows including Anthony Bourdain's No Reservations and the Netflix series, Taco Chronicles. The place has changed since Bourdain visited. They now have a dining room so you no longer have to stand on the street while you eat your taco, but the tacos are big and tasty as ever and they're still open in the wee hours of the night when those 3am munchies strike. Feel free to be adventurous and try something you've never heard of, but do be aware that some of those "unusual sounding" tacos contain gizzards, tongue, ears or other parts of the animal unfamiliar to foreign visitors. They might be delicious, but are you bold enough to find out?

listings.name: Mercado San Juan Arcos de Belen
listings.content: It is full of food stalls offering all the Mexican favorites. Find the one opposite the small bakers by one of the rear entrances on Calle Delicias, which serves the Torta Cubana. The people running it are amazingly welcoming and the food, especially the Cubana, is excellent.

listings.name: Don Toribio
listings.content: Delicious traditional Mexican cuisine at some of the best prices in Centro.

listings.name: Roldan 37
listings.content: Cozy upstairs restaurant specializing in chiles rellenos, including the national dish of chile en nogada. Very authentic cooking with several regional dishes based on indigenous traditions, and sometimes unusual ingredients that will offend the tastes of unsuspecting foreigners who might not appreciate the chance to eat grasshoppers. Though rest assured, there are plenty of "normal" dishes to choose from.

listings.name: Cafe el Popular
listings.content: Long-time fixture in the heart of downtown. Traditional homemade Mexican food including fresh baked breads, though the restaurant is historically Chinese and once served hybrid Mexicanized Chinese dishes. The place is known for its coffee and of course is a dependable source of good, hearty food when the midnight munchies strike.

listings.name: Chung King
listings.content: Generous plates, many of which are ramen. Spicy red chili sauce is provided for people who want to take the flavor up a notch.

listings.name: Kang Qing
listings.content: Buffet style restaurant with to-go service at 65 pesos, making it very cheap for a lot of food.

listings.name: Bufet Comida China
listings.content: Chinese buffet serving lots of food at low prices.

listings.name: El Huequito Bolivar
listings.content: This taco joint is good if you want to try tacos al pastor, as featured in Anthony Bourdain's Mexico show.

listings.name: Cafeteria El Cuadrilatero
listings.content: This torteria is owned by former luchador Super Astro, and serves not only tortas but also standard Mexican fare. Their enormous torta Super Gladiator is free if you can eat the whole thing in 15 minutes.

listings.name: La Opera Bar
listings.content: This restaurant has been serving Mexican food since the early 1900s and retains the same furniture since then. When you get there, look up to the ceiling, as you will see the famous gun shot accidentally fired by Pancho Villa.

listings.name: El Ehden
listings.content: This restaurant is favored by the local Mexican-Lebanese community, many of whom still own the small businesses and textile shops in the immediate area. It serves a range of standard Lebanese dishes, including an excellent mezze.

listings.name: El Mayor
listings.content: A newer rooftop establishment with great seating overlooking the Templo Mayor, this restaurant specializes in creative twists to traditional Mexican dishes. It's very popular for lunch, so it's best to arrive early.

listings.name: Hostería de Santo Domingo
listings.content: Housed in a former inn, this restaurant opened in 1860 and is the oldest restaurant in Mexico City. It serves classic traditional Mexican dishes in a lively atmosphere, and is very popular with residents.

listings.name: El Cardenal
listings.content: Upscale dining room serving outstanding regional and traditional Mexican cuisine. The restaurant has been a favorite of businessmen and politicos for generations. The food is always excellent, as is the service. They bake their own breads, offer several moles, offer unusual entrees, and are famous for their hot chocolate. Can be crowded weekdays for lunch and Sunday mornings. This listing is near the Zócalo, other locations are 1) about 100 meters from Palacio de Bellas Artes at Marconi 2, and 2) at the Sheraton hotel.

listings.name: Dulcería de Celaya
listings.content: This confectionery shop sells old fashioned sweets. It was established in 1874 and still has its original cabinets from that age.

listings.name: Limosneros
listings.content: Elegantly rustic dining room with innovative regional cuisine and a full bar with a variety of mezcals, tequilas, and an excellent wine list featuring many great Baja vintages. Adventurous palates shouild try the carnitas de conejo.

listings.name: Paxia
listings.content: Elegant rooftop restaurant with innovative nuevo Mexican cuisine and spectacular views of the historic downtown area.

listings.name: Testal
listings.content: Trendy casual restaurant serving traditional Mexican and regional dishes. Great breakfast and interesting dishes at lunch and dinner including nogales en chile, mole and more. Family friendly with affordable prices.

listings.name: Café de Tacuba
listings.content: Housed in a former convent, this institution serves up tasty Mexican dishes all day for reasonable prices. It is very popular so arrive early. Menu is in English and Spanish.

listings.name: La Terraza
listings.content: Restaurant on the roof of the Hotel Majestic overlooking the Zócalo, with stunning panoramic views of the city.

listings.name: Los Girasoles
listings.content: Traditional Mexican cuisine from various regions. Expect dishes like mole oaxqueno and if you're adventurous, chapulines. Pleasant outdoor patio on a plaza made for people watching. Mariachis on weekends.

listings.name: Miralto
listings.content: Many places in the Centro Histórico boast of the views from their rooftop dining rooms, but Miralto in the 41st floor of the Torre Latinoamericana looks down on all of them. Best views of any dining room in the city. Traditional Mexican cuisine is good, but unexceptional compared to the city's top restaurants.

listings.name: Azul Histórico
listings.content: Azul offers upscale Mexican cuisine in a romantic Centro courtyard with lush trees and stone archways.

listings.name: Masala y Maiz
listings.content: Elegant restaurant serving a fusion of contemporary Mexican cuisine with flavors and ingredients from Africa and India. Dishes are often unusual combinations like a paratha quesadilla, or a chai tres leches. Service is top notch. Reservations recommended. The restaurant was awarded a Michelin star in 2025.

listings.name: Balcon del Zocalo
listings.content: Rooftop dining atop the Hotel Zocalo Central. Food is nouveau Mexican with a number of unusual and creative fusions. The 9-course tasting menu is recommended because it highlights small plates showcasing various chef selections. The views are the best in the city with the Catedral Metropolitano and the Palacio Nacional lying just below (the night views make great photos with everything lit up). Very tourist friendly with English menus available, many English speaking waiters and the flexibility to suggest dishes for vegans.

listings.name: Salón Tenampa
listings.content: The original and most famous Mexican cantina, traditional home to the bohemians and mariachis of the 40s and 50s. Huge selection of tequila and mezcal, light Mexican food, and mariachi bands.

listings.name: La Opera
listings.content: Traditional bar dating back to the Porfiriato era (est. 1870), it's ornate and impressive to see, but a fun place to have a beer or a cocktail. Serves food.

listings.name: Salón España
listings.content: Old school traditional cantina where the tequila is strong and the men drink lots of it. They have mezcal and other liquors as well, but tequila is king here with more than 150 brands at your call! Free botanas (including tacos and quesadillas) while you continue drinking.

listings.name: Bar La Giaconda
listings.content: Casual place with good baguette sandwiches and dark draft beer.

listings.name: Sunday Sunday
listings.content: While the lightweights are nursing their hangovers on Sunday, the hardcore head to Mexico City's biggest Sunday night party where the house keeps rocking until 2am. The biggest crowds hit after midnight.

listings.name: Salon Corona
listings.content: Friendly traditional cantina since 1928. Popular place to watch a soccer game or hang out and drink beer. Serves traditional Mexican food.

listings.name: La Faena
listings.content: Old school cantina that celebrates the hispanic tradition of bullfighting. Campy wall decorations, a great jukebox full of classic Mexican rancheras, rock en espanol, and pop hits of the 90s. Cheap tacos, great variety of mezcal and tequila drinks, and a very lively crowd.

listings.name: Bosforo
listings.content: Dim, smoky bar with a hipster crowd. No sign, so you need to know where it is then look for the curtain across the doorway. Go in and join the crowd in sampling one of the city's widest selection of mezcals.

listings.name: Cantina Tio Pepe
listings.content: Traditional cantina with an early 20th-century vibe. Friendly atmosphere, occasional mariachis.

listings.name: Pulquería Las Duelistas
listings.content: Friendly and colorful traditional pulqueria (one of the most popular in the city) with murals on the ceiling and walls. Serves cured and white (blanco) pulques. Try a natural pulque to taste pure agave flavor, or try one of the fruit or spiced flavors. The celery (apio) is recommended.

listings.name: La Joya
listings.content: This used to be the Xochitl Pulqueria, but it changed hands in 2020 while keeping the tacky decor and the limited menu of just the pulques, only the pulques, and nothing but pulques, so help me God. Natural and curadas are available with flavors that include spices, fruits, and nuts.
listings.address: Eligio Ancona 122, Santa Maria La Ribera

listings.name: Marrakech Salon
listings.content: Wonderfully tacky flaming gay bar with drag queens and strippers for entertainment, no cover charge for anyone, and some delicious house mezcal drinks. Try the El Mayate --- minty and refreshing!

listings.name: La Purisima
listings.content: Delightfully tacky strip shows and disco balls. Very friendly crowd.

listings.name: Cafe Equis
listings.content: In business at the same location since 1930, this is Mexico City's oldest coffee house. They roast their own beans, specializing in organic Mexican-grown coffees. Cups of joe are also available for as little as M$15. The Cafe Veracruzano is sinfully delicious with a flavor of caramelized burnt sugar. Cash only.

listings.name: Cafe Regina
listings.content: Good coffee drinks plus hot chocolate and tea. Light food available including baked goods and vegetarian dishes like ratatouille.

listings.name: Café La Habana
listings.content: Opened in 1952, this iconic café is a nostalgic gem, steeped in history as a meeting place for revolutionaries like Fidel Castro and Che Guevara, who reportedly planned the Cuban Revolution here, and literary giants like Gabriel García Márquez and Roberto Bolaño, who frequented it during the 1970s infrarrealist movement. With its high ceilings, sepia-toned photos of Havana, and vintage coffee machine, it retains a 1950s ambiance. The menu features classic Mexican dishes like enchiladas and chilaquiles (though food quality varies), but the coffee—especially the café lechero (espresso with hot milk) or café bombón (double espresso with ground coffee)—is the star.
listings.price: M$69–140 for breakfast packages, coffee from M$30

listings.name: Hotel San Francisco
listings.content: Sparsely furnished, inexpensive rooms.

listings.name: Hotel Tuxpan
listings.content: A very good deal. Clean with cable TV, nice restrooms, and mirrors on the ceiling.

listings.name: Mexico City Hostel
listings.content: Breakfast included, Internet, laundry, lockers, tours and tourist information.

listings.name: Casa de los Amigos
listings.content: Established in the 1950s by the Quaker community in Mexico City, the Casa continues to be actively involved in local activities with a stated mission of promoting peace and international understanding. They run an affordable guest house (with either private rooms or dorm beds) with a two-night minimum, and is popular with international students or volunteers on extended stays, though there are still many who are "just tourists."

listings.name: Hostel Mundo Joven Catedral
listings.content: A clean and safe upscale hostel. Some rooms have partial views of the rear of the cathedral, but these are noisy due to the church bells. Discount with a Hosteling International card.

listings.name: Hotel Juarez
listings.content: A well taken care of hotel. Large rooms, TV, phone (free local calls) and private bathroom. Rooms may not all have windows.

listings.name: Hotel Principal
listings.content: Clean, friendly, and well run hotel with a range of rooms. Most overlook a quiet inner courtyard.

listings.name: Cadillac Hotel Boutique
listings.content: Stylish artsy place, very modern with excellent free breakfast. No A/C so better choice for winter than summer.

listings.name: Hotel Metropol
listings.content: Dated hotel that could use some redecorating tips, but rooms are spacious, they serve a buffet breakfast.

listings.name: Gran Hotel Ciudad de México
listings.content: This building built in 1899 was once a luxurious shopping center. It was converted into a hotel in 1966. The lobby of this place was featured in the film Frida.

listings.name: Best Western Hotel Majestic
listings.content: The location is great, the rooms are clean and comfortable but the service is vaudevillian. The restaurant on the top floor has a superb view of the Cathedral and Presidential Palace but the food isn't worthy of the atmosphere.

listings.name: Castillo de Chapultepec y Museo Nacional de Historia (MNH)
listings.content: The imposing castle on top of the hill calls to visitors. Over its history, it has been the home of the Spanish Viceroys, a military college, a scene of historic battle during the Mexican-American War, the palace of Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlotta, the national observatory, and the presidential palace. It is now a museum. You can walk about 1 km up the winding hill road, or take the tram that departs every twenty minutes for M$13. There are two parts to the museum: the Alcazar (with the exhibits on the life of its former residents – the emperor and the presidents), and the Castillo (now the Museum of National History). Both are decorated with remarkable murals depicting the nation's and the site's history. Don't miss the Roman-style gardens and observatory on the roof of the Alcazar. The castle also boasts a fine view of Mexico City and its surroundings. While visiting the site, you can leave your bag in the locker room for a fee near the entry to the site (at the bottom of the hill). Storing your bag is mandatory if it contains any food, and you will need to empty your water bottle at the top.
listings.price: Adult M$210, Mexican citizens and residents M$105 (ID required); seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays for Mexican citizens and residents; video camera and flash photography is not permitted

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Arte Moderno
listings.content: It showcases temporary exhibitions of Mexican and international art, and has a permanent collection of work by artists including Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, David Siqueiros, José Orozco, and Leonora Carrington, among others.

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
listings.content: One of the top anthropology museums in the world. This enormous complex highlights the development and cultures of Mexico's many indigenous peoples from thousands of years ago to today, and is full to the brim with ancient artifacts and artwork. Also, the museum itself is famous for its architecture. It is possible to spend days here to see everything – allocate two hours at the very least, prioritize your specific interests, and be sure not to miss the Aztec sun stone in the big room at the end of the plaza. Interpretive signage is underwhelming and mostly in Spanish - you'll enjoy the museum more if you go just to enjoy the ancient artwork rather than to get a history lesson. Bags must be checked; personal photography is permitted (no flash or tripods). If possible it is best to avoid visiting on Sundays, when it is usually mobbed. There is a restaurant on-site.
listings.price: Adult M$210, Mexican citizens and residents M$105 (ID required); seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays for Mexican citizens and residents
listings.address: Av Paseo de la Reforma y Calzada Gandhi s/n

listings.name: Museo Rufino Tamayo
listings.content: The original collection of this modern art museum was donated by the late Oaxacan-Zapoteca artist Rufino Tamayo and his wife, and includes works by Picasso, Rothko, and Miró, Georgia O'Keefe and many others. The collection also includes works from pre-Hispanic civilizations and works by Tamayo himself. Tamayo was heavily influenced by pre-Hispanic cultures, as were other modern artists in Mexico during the 20th century. The museum is handicap accessible with elevators, ramps, and loaner wheelchairs available. An upscale on-site restaurant includes an outdoor garden dining area. An on-site museum store has a good variety of books, prints, and contemporary art objects.
listings.price: Adult M$95; seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays

listings.name: Sala de Arte Publico Siqueiros
listings.content: This museum showcases the works of famed Mexican muralist David Alfaro Siquerios.
listings.price: M$12 adults; free for students, teachers, seniors, children under 12; free admission on Sundays

listings.name: Zoologico de Chapultepec
listings.content: Large, modern zoo in the same style as major ones in the U.S., famous for its pandas. Very crowded on weekends. Highlights for foreign visitors are the Anfibium axolotl center showcasing the unique endangered salamanders native to Mexico City, and the tropical forests section which is relatively uncrowded and has a large proportion of animals native to Mexico and Central America, like jaguars, spider monkeys, and tapirs. Backpacks are allowed inside, but not food or drinks (a bottle of water may or may not be allowed). It is customary to stop first at the vendors outside the entrance to buy a toy spider monkey ("changuito") to wear on your head during your visit.
listings.price: Free except for the butterfly or reptile houses

listings.name: Monumento a los Niños Héroes
listings.content: This impressive white marble monument stands at the entrance to Chapultepec Park in front of the Castillo. It honors six youths who gave their lives defending the stronghold from US troops in 1847. In the most dramatic telling of the legend, a cadet jumped to his death wrapped in the Mexican flag rather than surrendering to the American troops.

listings.name: Casa Gilardi
listings.content: Outstanding house tour that will appeal to anyone interested in modern architecture. The house was designed by world famous architect Luis Barragan (whose nearby home and studio is a ). Casa Gilardi is one of Barragan's signature projects, a private home that incorporates his concepts of human livability, integration with nature, and his bold use of brilliant colors and juxtaposed shapes. Reservations must be made in advance (can be done on the web site) and the house is open only for scheduled times. Tours are guided in small groups for an intimate, unrushed experience.

listings.name: Baths of Moctezuma
listings.content: A system of tanks, reservoirs, canals and waterfalls constructed by the Aztecs.

listings.name: Museo de Historia Natural y Cultura Ambiental
listings.content: Exhibits a history of evolution, with dinosaurs, whales, viruses, bugs, plants, human organs and more. If it's natural, it's here.
listings.price: M$23 adults; M$11 teachers, students, children 3-12; free for seniors, disabled, children under 3; free admission on Tuesday
listings.address: Bosque de Chapultepec II, Circuíto Correr es Salud s/n
listings.image: Museo de Historia Natural y Cultura Ambiental 04.jpg

listings.name: Luis Barragán House and Studio
listings.content: The home and studio of the famed Mexican architect Luis Barragán has been turned into a museum dedicated to his life and work. The house looks plain from the outside, but inside it opens up and exemplifies Barragan's modernist design philosophy of integrating light, and nature with open, aesthetically pleasing spaces and surfaces to create a serene and functional living space for humans. It is a .
listings.price: M$400 adults, M$300 Mexican citizens, M$200 students
listings.address: Gral. Francisco Ramírez 12, Ampliación Daniel Garza, Miguel Hidalgo, CDMX

listings.name: Panteon Civil de Dolores
listings.content: Largest cemetery in Mexico, site of the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons. The cemetery has over 1 million grave sites. People are just dying to get in here!

listings.name: Museo del Dolores de Cárcamo
listings.content: Small museum housed in a historic waterworks building, it houses a famous mural by Diego Rivera that could be considered a work of sculpture because part of it is a 3-dimensional bust while part of it is a tile mosaic mural covered by water.
listings.address: Av. Rodolfo Neri Vela, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc

listings.name: Los Pinos
listings.content: Mexico's "White House", which isn't white, but is the official residence of recent presidents. Since Andres Lopez Obrador was elected president in 2018, he and his successor have chosen to live in the Capitol building (Palacio Nacional), believing Los Pinos to be too opulent for a Mexican public servant. That decision leaves the official residence and grounds open for public tours and cultural events. Los Pinos is actually referred to as a "complex" because it isn't just one building, but rather several, in a quiet, natural area of Chapultepec Park. The presidential residence is the Casa Lazaro Cardenas, a grand 2-story mansion with marble floors, a sweeping grand staircase, and huge windows creating a bright, cheery atmosphere. When heads of state would come to visit, they would be invited to stay in a separate mansionː either the Casa Miguel Aleman or the Casa Adolfo Ruiz Cortines. The complex also includeds nature trails, tennis courts, and a helicopter pad. Today, the complex hosts outdoor concerts and cultural performances, workshops in cooking and regional arts, and other cultural activities.
listings.address: Calz. del Rey S/N, Bosque de Chapultepec I Secc

listings.name: Papalote Childrens Museum
listings.content: Cutting edge hands-on childrens activities to nurture young minds

listings.name: Museo Nacional de Energía y Tecnología
listings.content: Planes, trains and automobiles. Pretty much any other kind of machine too, from steam engines of the industrial age to AI and the robotics of tomorrow. Great place for teens!
listings.address: Av. de los Compositores s/n, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc

listings.name: Ex-Fabrica de Polvora
listings.content: Built by the Spanish military at the end of the colonial era; it is now used for cultural exhibits.

listings.name: Lago de Chapultepec
listings.content: There are actually two lakes that are connected, a bridge spanning them at mid-point. Lounge around the shore, or rent a canoe or paddleboat to explore.
listings.image: Lago de Chapultepec Torres Genelas de Polanco.jpg

listings.name: Lanchacinema
listings.content: A large movie screen is set up on the shore of Lake Chapultepec and movie goers sit in paddle boats in the lake to watch the movies. The movies are shown on a sporadic schedule, so consult current park info to see if a movie night is taking place during your visit to the city.

listings.name: Parque Aztlan
listings.content: Modern urban theme park opened in 2024. Thrill rides like roller coaster, swing, giant Ferris wheel and more. Requires a rechargeable card to pay for rides, which cost up to M$120 per ride. Restrooms cost M$5 to use (also paid via rechargeable card). Variety of concessions.
listings.price: Free, fees for each ride vary
listings.address: Av. de los Compositores s/n, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc

listings.name: Jardín Botánico
listings.content: 5.3 hectare garden showcasing more than 300 species of native Mexican plant life.

listings.name: Pista el Sope
listings.content: Wide running tracks and trails with mixed elevations. Groomed, chipped clay surface. Warm up area. Very popular among local runners and fitness enthusiasts.

listings.name: Auditorio Nacional
listings.content: Venue for performing arts and popular entertainers. Shows include family friendly events like the Nutcracker Suite, Placido Domingo, and Disney on Ice as well as popular Latin and international performers including Chayanne and Gilberto Santa Rosa. Seats 10,000. Tickets available through TicketMaster.

listings.name: Campo Marte
listings.content: Officially a military sports field owned by the Ministry of Defense (SEDENA), this is a well-known polo field where prestigious international matches have taken place, including the World Polo Championship in 2008 and the Prince of Wales Cup in 1993 (attended by Prince Charles, now King Charles). The regular polo season runs from November through April. Information about polo events and teams is available through the Federacion Mexicana Polo].

listings.name: Bistro Chapultepec
listings.content: Elegant lakeside dining in Chapultepec park, outdoor dining area available. Menu is more American or European than Mexican, which may appeal to some travelers. Reservations accepted.
listings.address: Lago Mayor, Secc. II, Bosque de Chapultepec

listings.name: Del Bosque
listings.content: Casual upscale dining with traditional Mexican cuisine. The restaurant is in Chapultepec Park, with a lakeside setting. The dining rooms features a glass wall with views of the lake right outside the restaurant.
listings.address: Lago Menor, Del Rosal s/n, Bosque De Chapultepec

listings.name: City Café Natural El Sope
listings.content: Casual outdoor cafe specializing in coffee and breakfast. Popular with runners and dog walkers alike. Very pet friendly with an area set aside for customers with well-behaved, leashed dogs.
listings.address: Av. de los Corredores S/N, Sección II, Bosque de Chapultepec

listings.name: Lago/Algo
listings.content: Sophisticated upscale dining in a landmark of modern architecture built on the edge of one of the lakes in Chapultepec Park. A cross between elegant dining and a cultural center that includes a gallery of contemporary art and spaces for cultural events. The menu is contemporary international cuisine with European favorites and seafood specialties that are less common in Mexico (like mussels). Tables can be reserved on Opentable.
listings.address: Bosque de Chapultepec, Pista El Sope S/N, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc

listings.name: Alfredo di Roma
listings.content: This is a charming and luxurious restaurant which serves slightly expensive Italian fare that is surprisingly worth it. Be sure to try the Fettuccine Alfredo or the Torre de Pisa, which is mouth-wateringly delicious.

listings.name: Comal Oculto
listings.content: Small traditional restaurant serving antojitos and other light fare. The house specialty is roasted pork shoulder tacos.

listings.name: Mari Gold
listings.content: Deliciously fascinating fusion of nouveau Mexican cuisine and Indian cuisine served in an elegantly sparse contemporary dining room. While the sabudana vada is recommended, most dishes will be unfamiliar to diners so a wise approach is to talk to the staff and trust in their recommendations.
listings.address: Calle Gob.Protasio Tagle 66A, San Miguel Chapultepec II Secc

listings.name: La Milla
listings.content: Small streetside cafe with a few tables outside on the sidewalk and more upstairs on a 2nd floor balcony. Wide range of pastries and baked goods, including several options for vegans. Excellent coffee.
listings.address: Calle Gral. Fco. Molinos del Campo 19

listings.name: Fiesta Americana Grand Chapultepec
listings.content: The location of the Fiesta American Grand Chapultepec is perfect, being close to the restaurants of Polanco and Condesa. Rooms are clean, quiet and very comfortable.

listings.name: JW Marriott Mexico City
listings.content: One of the premier Mexico City hotels, the JW Marriott Hotel Mexico City rises 26 stories high in the exclusive Polanco District. Located in the heart of the business and entertainment sector, this flagship Mexico City hotel is within walking distance to Auditorio Nacional, the city's financial hub, and some of Mexico's best shopping, dining and night life.

listings.name: Green Park Hotel
listings.content: Comfortable upscale hotel with traditional furnishings. Located adjacent to Chapultepec Park.
listings.address: Av Costituyentes 99, Col San Miguel Chapultepec,

listings.name: Hotel Atlantico
listings.content: Older budget hotel with spacious but minimalist rooms with worn furnishings.
listings.address: Av Observatorio 218, Daniel Garza al Poniente

listings.name: Hotel Park Villa
listings.content: Moderate hotel with dated facilities that cry out for renovation and update. Staff are friendly and location is good, across the street from Chapultepec Park and short walk to restaurants and bars of Condesa. Complimentary bicycles.
listings.address: Calle Gral. Gómez Pedraza 68, San Miguel Chapultepec

listings.name: Hotel Alexander
listings.content: Modern luxury hotel with spacious, comfortable rooms, well-equipped gym, good breakfast included in rate. First-class service with understated elegance.
listings.address: Bosque de Chapultepec, Lomas - Virreyes, Pedregal 24, Miguel Hidalgo

listings.name: Torres de Satelite
listings.content: Designed by famous Mexican architect Luis Barragan and built in 1957.

listings.name: Los Remedios National Park
listings.content: Popular park for jogging, working out, horseback riding and dog walking. About 900 hectares, mostly wooded with wide, marked trails.
listings.address: Calle Morelos Manzana 007, Bosque de los Remedios

listings.name: Sanctuary of the Virgin of Los Remedios
listings.content: One of the oldest basilicas in all the country. It's a nice spot to visit and the little town there is exceptional to bargain if you are in search of local art.

listings.name: Parque Naucalli
listings.content: State park with picnic areas, walking trails, skatepark, vendors, dinosaur exhibit. Occasional special events like a Christmas market.
listings.address: Perif. Blvd. Manuel Ávila Camacho Manzana 020, Boulevares

listings.name: Puerto Madero
listings.content: Casual Argentinian steakhouse that also serves seafood.

listings.name: La Vaka
listings.content: Steakhouse offering a variety of grilled meats including picaña, ribeyes and more. A buffet offers salads, pastas, soup, and traditional Mexican dishes.
listings.address: Boulevard Manuel Ávila Camacho Norte Conjunto

listings.name: Los Chatos
listings.content: Inexpensive casual restaurant serving traditional Mexican cuisine including arrachera, pozole and enchiladas. Homemade desserts.

listings.name: La Casa de los Olivos
listings.content: Casual restaurant serving traditional Mexican dishes including chile en nogada, milanesa, and various styles of chicken. The ribeye sandwich is both big and delicious.

listings.name: McCarthy's Irish Pub
listings.content: Basic corporate-style chain bar with several imported beers available. Dart boards and TVs tuned to sports games. Unexciting, but generically inoffensive.

listings.name: Fiesta Inn Naucalpan
listings.content: Roadside inn with large rooms.
listings.address: Periférico Norte, Av. Dr. Gustavo Baz esq, Alce Blanco

listings.name: Krystal Maria Barbara Hotel
listings.content: Comfortable hotel with rooms set around a large central courtyard featuring an outdoor swimming pool with a jacuzzi. On-site restaurant is available and you can take your meal inside the dining room our outdoors on the patio. Rooms are large, clean, and well-equipped.

listings.name: Hotel Real Hacienda Tlalnepantla
listings.content: Basic road travel hotel with modester accommations at reasonable prices.

listings.name: Casa Museo Leonora Carrington
listings.content: Home and studio of surrealist feminist artist Leonora Carrington. Born in Britain, Carrington lived in this Mexico City home for 60 years -- almost all of her artistically prolific career. Carrington is difficult to classify. She worked in Mexico, but was educated and raised in Great Britain, so she had none of the sense of "Mexicanidad" (Mexican identity) that permeates most modern art in Mexico. She was a surrealist and her work is best understood in an international context though she was readily accepted into the Mexican artistic community. A fascinating person and an immense talent.

listings.name: Museo del Juguete Antiguo México
listings.content: Huge collection of toys including dolls, action figures, model cars and trains, Barbies and lots more. Also provides walls to graffiti artists and is a popular place for urban artists to congregate.

listings.name: Museo del Objeto (MODO)
listings.content: Delightfully quirky museum of "stuff". All the things that become important to people in today's society, from toys, to car decorations. The museum is exhibition focused with changing themes a few times each year so the museum is "evergreen" and never the same place twice. It closes for several weeks every few months to change exhibits, so check their web site to verify that they're open and what the current exhibition theme is. Past themes have included "Objects of Literature", "Gol! Objects of Futbol" (soccer). Small museum that's fun and won't take more than an hour to explore.

listings.name: Casa Guillermo Tovar de Teresa
listings.content: Period home dating from 1910. Guillermo Tovar de Teresa was a respected intellectual in early 20th century Mexico and was a noted literary figure who chronicled life in Mexico City. The home and its furnishings, including an eclectic art collection, were purchased by the Carlos Slim Foundation. The home was restored and opened for public tours. It is operated by the Museo Soumaya (whose main museum is in Polanco). Allow about 1-2 hours for a visit.

listings.name: OMR
listings.content: Six to eight different exhibitions rotate throughout the year in this converted house in the heart of the Roma district, focusing on contemporary art by emerging Mexican artists.
listings.address: Plaza Río de Janeiro 54, Col. Roma

listings.name: 54 Gallery
listings.content: Modern gallery showcasing contemporary art (often avant garde pieces in non-traditional media). Many of the works are by established international artists, but there are also some pieces by well-known contemporary Mexico City artists that are quite often better than the overhyped, overpriced pieces from New York or Europe.

listings.name: MAIA Contemporary
listings.content: Quiet 2-story gallery with a gorgeous spiral staircase. Features contemporary works by many of the city's most talented artists.

listings.name: Mooni
listings.content: Casual gallery with friendly, informative staff. Affordable prices on a large selection of contemporary art, most by local Mexico City artists.
listings.address: Fernando Montes de Oca 43, Colonia Condesa

listings.name: Parque México
